flashcards.q: Walk through the three-way handshake with sequence numbers for client ISN=1000, server ISN=5000.
flashcards.a: SYN(seq=1000) -> SYN-ACK(seq=5000, ack=1001) -> ACK(ack=5001). SYN consumes one sequence number even with zero payload bytes.
CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN_SENT, SYN_RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT_1, FIN_WAIT_2, CLOSE_WAIT, CLOSING, LAST_ACK, TIME_WAIT.

flashcards.q: What does a pileup of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT mean?
flashcards.a: The peer sent a FIN and the kernel acked it, but the local application never called close(). This is an application resource leak, essentially never a network problem.

flashcards.q: Why does TIME_WAIT exist? Give both reasons.
flashcards.a: 1) Absorb any delayed duplicate segment from this exact connection so it can't be misdelivered into a new connection reusing the same 4-tuple. 2) Ensure the final ACK is retransmittable if the peer's LAST_ACK-state FIN retransmission arrives because the original ACK was lost.

flashcards.q: What is TIME_WAIT's duration per RFC 793 theory vs actual Linux implementation?
flashcards.a: RFC 793 assumes MSL=2min so 2xMSL=4min theoretically. Linux hardcodes TIME_WAIT to a flat 60 seconds (TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN), not configurable via sysctl, regardless of MSL assumptions.
tcp_fin_timeout (default 60s) governs how long an orphaned socket sits in FIN_WAIT_2 -- a different, distinct knob. It does not control TIME_WAIT's duration, which is hardcoded separately.

flashcards.q: Why is tcp_tw_recycle dangerous and removed from Linux?
flashcards.a: Removed in Linux 4.12+ because its safety check assumed monotonically increasing per-peer timestamps, which is false when multiple NATed clients share one source IP -- it silently drops legitimate connections from NATed clients.

FIN = graceful, ordered 'no more data from me, still can receive' -- part of normal state machine, consumes a sequence number. RST = abrupt abort, no delivery guarantee, discards buffers -- sent for SYN to a closed port, close() with unread buffered data, or SO_LINGER(0).

flashcards.q: Why does closing a socket with unread data trigger an RST instead of a clean FIN?
flashcards.a: A graceful close would silently discard the unread data; the kernel sends RST instead to signal the abnormal termination, which is why a client sees 'Connection reset by peer' after uploading a body a server rejected without draining it.

flashcards.q: How fast do TCP sequence numbers wrap at 10Gbps, and what protects against misinterpreting wrapped duplicates?
flashcards.a: 2^32 bytes / (10Gbps/8) ~= 3.4 seconds. PAWS (RFC 7323) uses the TCP timestamp option, a monotonically increasing per-segment value, to disambiguate old wrapped duplicates from new data.

flashcards.q: What's a half-close, and what socket call triggers it?
flashcards.a: One side sends FIN (stops sending, can still receive) while the connection stays open the other direction -- shutdown(SHUT_WR), distinct from close() which tears down both directions.

flashcards.q: State the RTO defaults: initial value, backoff behavior, and Linux's retry cap.
flashcards.a: Initial RTO = 1 second (RFC 6298), doubles (exponential backoff) per retransmit of the same segment. Linux tcp_retries2 defaults to 15, stretching to roughly 15-30 minutes worst case before the kernel reports the connection dead.

flashcards.q: Why is 'connection refused' fast and 'connection timeout' slow?
flashcards.a: Refused = a closed port immediately generates a kernel-level RST since the OS actively knows nothing is listening. Timeout = a firewall silently dropped the SYN, so the client just waits out its own retransmission/timeout with no signal at all.
